units.title: Measuring the Economy
units.blurb: The circular flow, what GDP counts and how it is added up, and how to separate real growth from rising prices.

units.title: Unemployment, Inflation and the Business Cycle
units.blurb: Who counts as unemployed, the kinds of unemployment, price indexes and inflation, who gains and loses from inflation, and the phases of the business cycle.

units.title: Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply
units.blurb: The AD–AS model: why each curve has its shape, what shifts it, the multipliers, short-run and long-run equilibrium, and how the economy adjusts.

units.title: Fiscal Policy
units.blurb: Government spending and taxes as tools against output gaps, how large a change is needed, tax structures, automatic stabilizers, and deficits and debt.

units.title: Money, Banks and the Central Bank
units.blurb: Financial assets and interest rates, what money is and how it is measured, how banks create it, the money market, the central bank's tools, monetary policy, and the loanable funds market.

units.title: Policy in the Long Run
units.blurb: Fiscal and monetary policy together, the Phillips curve, money growth and inflation, crowding out, and where schools of thought agree and differ.

units.title: Economic Growth
units.blurb: Productivity, the power of compound growth, and the policies that can raise growth over the long run.

units.title: The Open Economy
units.blurb: The balance of payments, exchange rates and the foreign exchange market, and how trade and capital flows tie economies together.

topics.title: The Circular Flow
topics.short: Households and firms meet in product and factor markets, with money flowing one way and goods and resources the other.
topics.trouble: Students put households on the selling side of the product market or the buying side of the factor market, or think money leaves the economy when it is spent.

topics.title: What GDP Counts
topics.short: GDP is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given period.
topics.trouble: Students count intermediate goods, used goods, stock purchases and transfer payments, which either counts things twice or counts things that were not newly produced.

topics.title: GDP = C + I + G + NX
topics.short: Sort spending into consumption, investment, government purchases and net exports, then add.
topics.trouble: Students treat buying stocks as investment (in GDP, investment means new capital goods, new homes and added inventories), and think imports are subtracted because they shrink GDP; they are subtracted because they were already counted in C, I or G.

topics.title: Value Added and the Income Approach
topics.short: Adding the value each stage of production adds, or adding everyone's income, gives the same total as final spending.
topics.trouble: Students add up the sales at every stage of production, counting the wheat again in the flour and again in the bread.

topics.title: GDP per Person and Its Limits
topics.short: GDP per person helps compare living standards, but it leaves out work at home, leisure, the environment and how income is shared.
topics.trouble: Students treat GDP as a complete measure of well-being, or compare total GDP across countries with very different populations.

topics.title: Nominal and Real GDP
topics.short: Real GDP values output at base-year prices, so it grows only when production grows.
topics.trouble: Students read a rise in nominal GDP as more production when it may be only higher prices.

topics.title: The GDP Deflator
topics.short: The deflator is nominal GDP divided by real GDP, times 100, and it turns nominal values into real ones.
topics.trouble: Students divide real GDP by nominal GDP, or forget the factor of 100, and get a deflator that is upside down or 100 times too small.

topics.title: Who Is in the Labor Force
topics.short: The labor force is everyone working plus everyone without a job who is looking for one.
topics.trouble: Students count every adult without a job as unemployed, including retirees, full-time students and discouraged workers who have stopped looking.

topics.title: The Unemployment Rate
topics.short: Divide the number unemployed by the labor force, not by the whole population.
topics.trouble: Students divide by the adult population, and do not see that discouraged workers leaving the labor force can lower the unemployment rate.

topics.title: Frictional, Structural and Cyclical Unemployment
topics.short: The natural rate is frictional plus structural unemployment; cyclical unemployment comes from recessions.
topics.trouble: Students think full employment means zero unemployment, or call a worker whose skills are no longer needed cyclically unemployed rather than structurally unemployed.

topics.title: Price Indexes and the CPI
topics.short: A price index compares the cost of a fixed basket of goods with its cost in a base year, set to 100.
topics.trouble: Students read an index of 120 as a price of 120 dollars, and miss that the CPI tends to overstate inflation because people switch to cheaper goods and quality improves.

topics.title: Inflation, Deflation and Disinflation
topics.short: The inflation rate is the percent change in a price index from one period to the next.
topics.trouble: Students think falling inflation means falling prices. Disinflation means prices still rise, only more slowly; deflation means they fall.

topics.title: Converting Nominal to Real
topics.short: Divide a dollar amount by the price index over 100 to compare dollars from different years.
topics.trouble: Students compare wages or prices from different decades in nominal dollars, or multiply by the index when they should divide.

topics.title: Who Gains and Loses from Inflation
topics.short: Unexpected inflation helps borrowers and hurts lenders and people on fixed incomes; all inflation brings menu costs and shoe-leather costs.
topics.trouble: Students think inflation makes everyone poorer by the inflation rate. When wages rise along with prices, real income need not fall, and surprise inflation moves buying power from lenders to borrowers.

topics.title: The Business Cycle
topics.short: Real GDP moves through expansion, peak, contraction and trough around its long-run trend.
topics.trouble: Students confuse slower growth with a recession, in which real output falls, or think potential output is the most an economy could ever produce; output can run above potential for a while.

topics.title: Aggregate Demand
topics.short: AD slopes down because of the wealth, interest-rate and exchange-rate effects, not because buyers switch to other goods.
topics.trouble: Students explain the slope of AD with the substitution effect from a single market. When the whole price level rises there is no cheaper good to switch to.

topics.title: What Shifts Aggregate Demand
topics.short: A change in consumption, investment, government purchases or net exports at every price level shifts AD.
topics.trouble: Students shift AD when the price level changes, which is a movement along AD.

topics.title: Marginal Propensities to Consume and Save
topics.short: MPC is the share of an extra dollar of income that is spent, MPS the share that is saved, and MPC + MPS = 1.
topics.trouble: Students compute the MPC as total spending over total income instead of the change in spending over the change in income.

topics.title: The Spending Multiplier
topics.short: New spending becomes someone's income and is partly spent again, so GDP rises by 1/(1 − MPC) times the first change.
topics.trouble: Students use the MPC itself as the multiplier, or divide 1 by the MPC instead of by the MPS.

topics.title: The Tax Multiplier
topics.short: A tax cut raises GDP by MPC/MPS times its size, less than the same increase in government purchases.
topics.trouble: Students use the spending multiplier for a tax change, forgetting that part of a tax cut is saved before any spending happens, or miss the sign: a tax increase lowers GDP.

topics.title: Short-Run Aggregate Supply
topics.short: SRAS slopes up because wages and some prices are slow to adjust; input prices, productivity and supply shocks shift it.
topics.trouble: Students shift SRAS when the price level changes, or treat higher input costs as an increase in SRAS because the curve moves up.

topics.title: Long-Run Aggregate Supply
topics.short: LRAS is vertical at full-employment output, which resources and technology set, not the price level.
topics.trouble: Students draw LRAS sloping up, or shift it when demand changes. LRAS moves only when the economy's capacity to produce changes.

topics.title: Equilibrium and Output Gaps
topics.short: Where AD meets SRAS, output may sit below full employment (a recessionary gap) or above it (an inflationary gap).
topics.trouble: Students mix up the two gaps, for example calling output above full employment a recessionary gap.

topics.title: Demand Shocks and Supply Shocks
topics.short: A demand shock moves the price level and output the same way; a supply shock moves them in opposite directions.
topics.trouble: Students expect every shock to raise prices and output together, and miss stagflation, where a negative supply shock raises prices while output falls.

topics.title: Long-Run Self-Adjustment
topics.short: Over time, wages and other input prices adjust and SRAS shifts until output returns to full employment.
topics.trouble: Students close a gap by shifting LRAS or AD, when the self-correcting move is a shift of SRAS. How quickly this happens is a question economists debate.

topics.title: Expansionary and Contractionary Fiscal Policy
topics.short: Raising spending or cutting taxes pushes AD right to close a recessionary gap; the reverse closes an inflationary gap.
topics.trouble: Students choose a tax increase to fight a recession, or count transfer payments as government purchases (transfers work like a tax cut).

topics.title: How Big a Fiscal Change?
topics.short: Divide the output gap by the right multiplier to find the change in spending or taxes needed.
topics.trouble: Students set the spending change equal to the whole output gap, ignoring the multiplier, or use the spending multiplier for a tax change.

topics.title: Progressive, Regressive and Proportional Taxes
topics.short: Marginal and average tax rates, and what happens to the average rate as income rises.
topics.trouble: Students think moving into a higher bracket taxes all of their income at the higher rate, so a raise could lower take-home pay. Only the dollars above the threshold face the higher marginal rate.

topics.title: Automatic Stabilizers
topics.short: Progressive income taxes and programs like unemployment insurance cushion recessions without any new law.
topics.trouble: Students call any recession-fighting spending an automatic stabilizer, including new laws passed after a recession starts, which are discretionary policy.

topics.title: Budget Deficits and the National Debt
topics.short: A deficit is one year's shortfall; the debt is the running total of past deficits minus surpluses.
topics.trouble: Students use deficit and debt as the same word, or think a shrinking deficit means the debt is falling.

topics.title: Bonds, Stocks and Interest Rates
topics.short: When market interest rates rise, the prices of existing bonds fall.
topics.trouble: Students think bond prices and interest rates move together, or that buying a bond makes you part owner of a company.

topics.title: Nominal and Real Interest Rates
topics.short: The real interest rate is about the nominal rate minus the inflation rate.
topics.trouble: Students add inflation instead of subtracting it, or think a lender earning 5% gains 5% in buying power when inflation is 3%.

topics.title: What Money Does
topics.short: Money is a medium of exchange, a unit of account and a store of value.
topics.trouble: Students call a credit card money (it is a way to borrow, and the loan is repaid with money), or think money must be backed by gold to work.

topics.title: Measuring Money: M1 and M2
topics.short: M1 holds the most liquid forms of money; M2 adds less liquid ones such as small time deposits.
topics.trouble: Students count stocks, bonds or unused credit limits as money, or think M1 and M2 are separate pools rather than M2 containing M1.

topics.title: Bank Balance Sheets
topics.short: Assets (reserves, loans, securities) equal liabilities (deposits) plus owners' equity; reserves split into required and excess.
topics.trouble: Students list deposits as a bank's assets. To the bank, a deposit is money it owes the depositor.

topics.title: How Banks Create Money
topics.short: When banks lend out excess reserves, new deposits appear; the simple money multiplier is 1 divided by the reserve ratio.
topics.trouble: Students think a cash deposit by itself raises the money supply (it only changes the form of money held), and apply the multiplier to the whole deposit instead of to the excess reserves.

topics.title: The Money Market
topics.short: The demand for money and the supply the central bank provides set the nominal interest rate.
topics.trouble: Students draw the money supply sloping up instead of vertical, or shift money demand when the interest rate changes, which is a movement along it.

topics.title: The Central Bank's Tools
topics.short: Open market operations, the discount rate, reserve requirements and the interest rate paid on reserves.
topics.trouble: Students think the central bank buys bonds to fight inflation. Buying bonds adds reserves and money, which is expansionary.

topics.title: Setting Rates with Ample Reserves
topics.short: When banks hold plenty of reserves, the Fed steers the federal funds rate mainly through the interest rate it pays on reserves.
topics.trouble: Students assume small open market operations still move the federal funds rate, as in the limited-reserves model. With ample reserves, administered rates do most of the work.

topics.title: Monetary Policy and the Economy
topics.short: Lower interest rates raise investment and consumption, shifting AD right; higher rates do the reverse.
topics.trouble: Students link the steps in the wrong order, or think the central bank directly sets every interest rate, mortgage rates included.

topics.title: The Loanable Funds Market
topics.short: Saving supplies and borrowing demands loanable funds, and together they set the real interest rate.
topics.trouble: Students mix up the money market (nominal rate, money supply and demand) with the loanable funds market (real rate, saving and borrowing), and shift the wrong curve when the government borrows.

topics.title: Fiscal and Monetary Policy Together
topics.short: Combine two policies' effects on output, the price level and interest rates, and spot which result is uncertain.
topics.trouble: Students give a definite answer when two policies push a variable in opposite directions. Then the result depends on their sizes.

topics.title: The Short-Run Phillips Curve
topics.short: In the short run, lower unemployment comes with higher inflation; an AD shift moves the economy along the curve.
topics.trouble: Students shift the short-run Phillips curve when AD changes. AD shifts move along it, while supply shocks and changes in expected inflation shift it.

topics.title: The Long-Run Phillips Curve
topics.short: In the long run, unemployment returns to its natural rate whatever the inflation rate, so the curve is vertical.
topics.trouble: Students treat the short-run tradeoff as permanent, believing a government can hold unemployment low forever by accepting higher inflation.

topics.title: Money Growth and Inflation
topics.short: MV = PY: in the long run, money growing faster than output raises prices.
topics.trouble: Students think printing more money makes a country richer in the long run. How stable velocity is, and so how close the link is from year to year, is debated.

topics.title: Crowding Out
topics.short: Government borrowing can raise the real interest rate and reduce private investment.
topics.trouble: Students shift the supply of loanable funds when the government borrows, instead of the demand. How much crowding out happens, especially when resources sit idle, is debated.

topics.title: Schools of Macroeconomic Thought
topics.short: Classical, Keynesian, monetarist and newer schools agree on much and differ on how fast markets adjust and how active policy should be.
topics.trouble: Students treat one school as right and the rest as wrong. Economists broadly agree on many points, such as money's neutrality in the long run, and debate others, such as how fast wages adjust and how active policy should be.

topics.title: Productivity and Growth
topics.short: Output per hour of work rises with physical capital, human capital and technology.
topics.trouble: Students credit growth to more hours of work alone, and miss that lasting gains in living standards come from more output per hour.

topics.title: Compound Growth and the Rule of 70
topics.short: At a growth rate of g percent a year, a quantity doubles in about 70/g years.
topics.trouble: Students add growth year by year instead of compounding it, so they badly underestimate how small differences in growth rates add up over decades.

topics.title: Policies for Long-Run Growth
topics.short: Policies that build physical capital, skills and technology shift LRAS and the PPC outward.
topics.trouble: Students think any boost to demand raises long-run growth. Spending that only shifts AD does not raise potential output unless it adds to the economy's capacity to produce.

topics.title: The Balance of Payments
topics.short: The current account and the capital and financial account record a country's dealings with the rest of the world, and they balance each other.
topics.trouble: Students think a trade deficit means money is draining out of the country, missing that it is matched by a financial account surplus as foreigners buy assets.

topics.title: Exchange Rates
topics.short: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another; a currency appreciates when it buys more of the other.
topics.trouble: Students read a rise in yen per dollar as the yen appreciating. It means the dollar has appreciated and the yen has depreciated.

topics.title: The Foreign Exchange Market
topics.short: Demand for dollars comes from foreigners buying U.S. goods and assets; supply comes from Americans buying foreign ones.
topics.trouble: Students forget the mirror market: when Europeans demand more dollars, they also supply more euros.

topics.title: What Moves Exchange Rates
topics.short: Tastes, relative incomes, relative price levels and relative interest rates shift the demand for and supply of a currency.
topics.trouble: Students expect higher U.S. inflation to strengthen the dollar. It makes U.S. goods dearer and tends to weaken the dollar.

topics.title: Exchange Rates and Net Exports
topics.short: A stronger currency makes exports dearer abroad and imports cheaper at home, lowering net exports and AD.
topics.trouble: Students assume a strong currency is always good for a country's output, missing its effect on exporters.

topics.title: Interest Rates and Capital Flows
topics.short: A higher real interest rate draws in foreign financial capital, which raises demand for the currency.
topics.trouble: Students expect a higher interest rate to weaken a currency because borrowing costs more. It draws foreign savers, who must buy the currency first.

topics.title: Saving, Investment and the Trade Balance
topics.short: Private saving plus the government's budget balance equals domestic investment plus net exports.
topics.trouble: Students treat the trade balance as separate from saving and investment. By the identity, the trade balance changes only if saving, investment or the government's budget balance changes too.
